slides.title: Python Basics
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter is the prompt, the values it computes with, the operators that combine them, the names that remember them, and a first program. Every concept gets an idea, a reason and a picture first, then the code, then what the run printed.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Four parts: values and types, operations, names and functions, and a first program. Each range is a run of slides you can jump to. The chapter-code tab of the page holds the same code in the same order. Ask the class which part they expect to find hardest, and why.

slides.title: Three questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Three questions to carry through the chapter. Which operations can raise an error, and which error? Which results can surprise a student? And what has changed in current Python since the book? Ask students to write a guess for each now and check it at the end.

slides.title: Part 1: Values and types
slides.say: Part one. The shell evaluates an expression and prints its value, and every value has a data type: integer, float or string. Example: seven plus one point zero is a float. Ask the class which result in this part they expect to surprise them.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: values and types
slides.say: A calculator with a screen is the shell. An expression is a recipe line that ends in one value. A data type is the label on a container. Example: the crate, the jug and the sign. Ask students to add an everyday picture of their own for a data type.

slides.title: The shell: type a line, read the value
slides.say: The shell reads an expression, computes its value and prints it. An expression is any code that ends in one value. Example: two plus three times six. Ask the class: is the answer twenty or thirty, and which rule decides?

slides.title: The shell: type an expression, get a value
slides.say: In a script you write print yourself, and the table shows each expression with its value and type. Predict two plus three times six before the run, and say why it is not thirty. Then change a number and run it again.

slides.title: Story: a Christmas hobby named after a comedy troupe
slides.say: Guido van Rossum began Python in the Christmas week of 1989 at CWI in Amsterdam, and the name comes from Monty Python, not the snake. Show the Wikipedia page for the date. Ask the class: what makes a language pleasant to read for a beginner?

slides.title: Data types: int, float and str
slides.say: Every value has a type that says what it is and what it can do. Example: seven is an int, three and a half is a float. Ask the class: what type does seven plus one point zero have, and why?

slides.title: Data types: int, float and str
slides.say: The function type names the type of any value. The table colours int, float and str, and the second group shows that one float turns the whole sum into a float. Ask the class to predict the type of seven plus one.

slides.title: Integers: exact, however large
slides.say: Python integers have no size limit, so they never overflow. Example: two to the power one hundred has thirty-one digits and is exact. Ask the class: what would a language with fixed-size integers print for it, and why does that matter?

slides.title: Integers never overflow
slides.say: The chart counts the digits of each result. Two to the power one hundred is written out in full. The function int reads text as a whole number and cuts a float without rounding. Ask the class what int of four point seven gives.

slides.title: Floats: close, not exact
slides.say: A float is stored in binary, so most decimals are only close. Example: zero point one plus zero point two is not exactly zero point three. Ask the class: why does a shop program never compare two floats with the equals sign?

slides.title: Floats are honest about being approximate
slides.say: The table marks the surprising line: the sum is not equal to zero point three. Rounding shows a tidy number, but the stored value stays unchanged. Division with a slash always gives a float. Ask the class what six divided by three prints.

slides.title: Strings: text between quotes
slides.say: A string is text between quotes, and len counts every character. Example: Hello, world has thirteen, because the comma, the space and the mark count too. Ask the class: is the text seven equal to the number seven, and how could you find out?

slides.title: Strings: text between quotes
slides.say: The picture counts the thirteen cells, letters in teal and marks in grey. The table shows why the text seven and the number seven are different values: Python never converts between them silently. Ask the class to predict the type of each.

slides.title: Part 2: Operations
slides.say: Part two. Operators combine values, precedence decides who goes first, and parentheses override it. Plus and star also work on strings, with a different meaning. Example: two plus three times six. Ask the class to predict it before the run.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: operators
slides.say: Operators are verbs between values. Precedence is the order of work in a kitchen: chop before you stir. Go through the eight pictures one by one. Example: folding paper doubles it, which is the power. Ask which picture the students remember best.

slides.title: Seven operators for numbers
slides.say: Python has seven arithmetic operators. Example: five divided by two gives two point five, and five floor-divided by two gives two. Ask the class: which operator pair would you use to split sweets between friends and then count the leftovers?

slides.title: Seven operators for numbers
slides.say: The table lists each operator with its result for five and two, and the bar chart draws them. The slash always gives a float. The double slash and the percent sign work as a pair. Ask the class to predict five to the power two.

slides.title: Precedence: who goes first
slides.say: Precedence is the order in which operators run. Example: two plus three times six is twenty, but with parentheses around two plus three it is thirty. Ask the class: why is minus three to the power two equal to minus nine?

slides.title: Who goes first: operator precedence
slides.say: The chart shows five expressions and their values, and the table lists the order of the operators. Power goes first, then times and divide, then plus and minus. Equal rank runs left to right. Ask the class to predict eight divided by two times three.

slides.title: Quotient and remainder
slides.say: Floor division counts full boxes and the remainder counts what is left. Example: twenty-three candies in boxes of seven fill three boxes and leave two. Ask the class: how can you check that the pair of answers is right, using only multiplication and addition?

slides.title: Division three ways: quotient and remainder
slides.say: The drawing sorts twenty-three candies into boxes of seven. Quotient times divisor plus remainder gives twenty-three back. Floor division rounds down, so minus seven by two is minus four, not minus three. Ask the class to predict minus seven percent two.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: operations on text
slides.say: Concatenation glues strips of text, and replication photocopies them. The function str is the label maker that turns any value into text. Example: gluing Alice to Bob. Ask the class why a glue stick cannot join a strip of paper to a number.

slides.title: Concatenation: + joins text
slides.say: Plus between two strings glues them without a space. Example: Alice plus Bob gives AliceBob. Python refuses to glue text to a number and raises a TypeError. Ask the class: which function turns the number forty-two into text, and where in the line does it go?

slides.title: String concatenation: + joins text
slides.say: The table shows four joins and marks the failing one. The error message names both types, which is the clue. The function str makes the number into text first, and then the join works. Ask the class to read the error aloud.

slides.title: Replication: * repeats text
slides.say: Star between a string and a whole number repeats the string. Example: Alice times three. Zero copies give the empty string, and a float count raises a TypeError. Ask the class: what does the order three times ab give, and does the order of the two matter?

slides.title: String replication: * repeats text
slides.say: The table lists the results and the chart counts their characters. The order of the string and the number does not matter. The count must be an integer, so Alice times two point five fails. Ask the class what the empty string looks like when printed.

slides.title: Part 3: Names and functions
slides.say: Part three. A variable is a name for a value. Print shows, input reads, and str, int, float and len convert and measure. Errors are answers too. Example: adding text to a number. Ask the class what Python will say before you run it.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: names
slides.say: A variable is a labelled jar: the label is the name, the contents are the value. Print is the loudspeaker, and input is the suggestion box. Example: a number dropped in the box arrives as paper. Ask the class why input gives text.

slides.title: Variables: names that remember
slides.say: A variable is a name that refers to a value. Example: spam equals forty-two, then spam equals spam plus one, and the jar now holds forty-three. Ask the class: why does Spam with a capital S fail, when spam with a small s works?

slides.title: Variables: names that remember
slides.say: The drawing moves the label from one value to the next. Names are case-sensitive, so Spam was never assigned and Python reports a NameError. Ask the class to predict what the third print shows, and then to run it and read the message aloud.

slides.title: print: the function that shows
slides.say: The function print writes its items separated by a space and ends the line. Example: Hello and world become Hello world. The options sep and end change the separator and the ending. Ask the class: what does print with nothing inside write?

slides.title: print: the function that shows
slides.say: The table shows the exact text each call writes, with a dot for each space and a mark for each line end. The amber chip is the separator and the green chip is the ending. Ask the class to change sep to a comma and predict the line.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: functions and modules
slides.say: Len is a ruler for text. Int and float are machines with a slot for the input and a slot for the result. Import fetches a toolbox from the shelf. Example: the machine int reads the text forty-two. Ask which machine rejects the text four point two.

slides.title: Conversions and len
slides.say: The functions str, int and float convert a value, and len counts characters. Example: str of twenty-nine is the text twenty-nine. Ask the class: why does len of the number twelve thousand three hundred forty-five fail, and what fixes it?

slides.title: Conversions and len: built-in functions
slides.say: The table lists each call, its result and the type of the result. The drawing shows a value going in and a converted value coming out. A number has no length, so str turns it into text first. Ask the class what int of four point seven gives.

slides.title: Errors are answers too
slides.say: An error name says what went wrong. A ValueError means the type is right but the content is not, as in int of the text four point two. A TypeError means the type itself does not fit. Ask the class: which error does len of a number raise?

slides.title: Errors are answers too
slides.say: The table shows an ordinary call and two failing calls with Python's own messages, and the drawing sorts them by cause. Read the name first, then the message. Ask the class to predict the error for int of the text hello.

slides.title: input always returns text
slides.say: The function input always returns text, even when the person types digits. Example: the text twenty plus the text one glues to two hundred and one. Ask the class: which function do you call before you calculate with it, and what does it return?

slides.title: input always returns text
slides.say: This example names the text input would return, so no keyboard is needed. The drawing follows the typed value into a string and then into a number. Plus on text glues, plus on numbers adds. Ask the class to predict each line.

slides.title: Modules: import opens a toolbox
slides.say: Import brings a module into your program, and a dot reaches inside it. Example: math dot sqrt of sixteen is four point zero, and math dot pi is the value of pi. Ask the class: why is the answer to a square root a float?

slides.title: Modules: import opens a toolbox
slides.say: The drawing shows the name math pointing at the module and the two things taken from it. The standard library is free and always installed. Ask the class to name one other module they have heard of and what it might hold.

slides.title: Part 4: A first program
slides.say: Part four. A first program uses everything so far. Then we take it apart line by line, and finish with the binary digits behind every number. Example: the greeting program. Ask the class which earlier idea they see in each of its lines.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: a program and its bits
slides.say: A program is a recipe: steps in order, ingredients in labelled jars. Dissecting it is taking a clock apart, and binary is a row of light switches. Example: five is the switches for four and one. Ask the class which picture helps them most.

slides.title: Story: where hello, world began, in 1972
slides.say: The first hello, world was in a 1972 tutorial for the language B, and the 1978 C book made it famous. In B the text needed three variables; in Python it is one line. Ask the class: what does a first program prove when it prints?

slides.title: Your first program
slides.say: The first program greets, asks, measures and calculates. Example: it keeps the name in a variable and builds the greeting with plus. Ask the class: which line would break if you forgot to convert the age to a number, and what would the error say?

slides.title: Your first program
slides.say: Because the page has no keyboard, the example names the text input would return. The table traces every line: what it shows and what it stores. Ask the class to change the name and the age and predict the output before the run.

slides.title: Dissecting the program
slides.say: Dissecting a program means reading it line by line and naming each part. Example: the same sentence built by joining five pieces, and by filling an f-string. Ask the class: which of the two would you rather read, and why?

slides.title: Dissecting the program: join or fill in
slides.say: The drawing breaks both lines into pieces: teal for text, amber for values. The f-string is shorter and needs no str. Both lines print the same sentence. Ask the class to add the city as a third slot and show both versions.

slides.title: Story: Leibniz wrote every number with only 0 and 1
slides.say: Leibniz described binary arithmetic in 1679, and Bouvet's letter from Peking in 1703 showed the I Ching hexagrams as binary numbers. Open the link and read out the dates. Ask the class: why would a machine prefer two digits to ten?

slides.title: Binary: numbers from 0 and 1
slides.say: Binary writes numbers with only zero and one, and each place is a power of two. Example: five is four plus one, written one zero one. Ask the class: how many different values fit in one byte, and how do you work that out?

slides.title: How computers store numbers: binary
slides.say: The picture shows the eight places of a byte and which ones are switched on for five. The function bin shows the digits, and int with base two reads them back. Ask the class to write ten in binary and check it with bin.

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. The shell and its error messages improved in 3.13, and the free-threaded build is experimental. F-strings have a formal grammar since 3.12. Example: PEP 701. Ask the class to check one row against its source before trusting it.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep, and the chart counts the code examples of each part. Everything is on the chapter page, in the same order. Example: the first sentence, the shell prints one value. Ask each student to say which sentence they still doubt.

slides.title: Practice questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run on the page. Example: seven floor-divided by two, times two, plus seven remainder two. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence to a neighbour, and to name the rule that decided it.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter and the Python tutorial, then the video by Guido van Rossum. The stories link to first-hand sources. Example: the floating-point page explains zero point one plus zero point two. Ask each student to choose one link to read before the next class.
